title: NASA's Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
summary:
NASA's Crew-13 mission was getting ready to launch. The SpaceX Dragon spacecraft was scheduled to lift off at 11:10 a.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 1, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Docking with the International Space Station was targeted for about 7 p.m. The planned journey from launch to docking would take 7 hours and 50 minutes. If it happened as scheduled, it would be the fastest trip to the space station by a U.S. spacecraft in the station's history.

Four crew members were to fly on Dragon. They are NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. They will spend an extended period aboard the station conducting science and other mission activities.

NASA planned to broadcast the mission across several platforms. Launch coverage was to begin at 9:20 a.m. After the main launch broadcast ends, NASA will provide audio-only communications involving Crew-13, the space station and flight controllers while Dragon travels toward the orbiting laboratory. A postlaunch news conference was set for 12:45 p.m. Arrival coverage was to begin at 5:20 p.m., with docking targeted for 7 p.m. at the forward-facing port of the station's Harmony module. Hatch opening followed by welcome remarks was planned for 8:45 p.m.

After entering the space station, the Crew-13 astronauts and cosmonaut will complete a brief handover with members of NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission. Crew-12 is expected to begin its journey back to Earth no earlier than Monday, Oct. 5. NASA plans to release further information about the Crew-12 return after Crew-13 has arrived at the station.

In-person events are limited to media representatives who have already received credentials. All times are Eastern and subject to change based on real-time operations.
why_it_matters: Crews rotate on the space station so science work can continue. A schedule shows how many steps, from launch to hatch opening, must fit together carefully.
